extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners (primary) and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and formulating rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 (subject matter eligibility), including when to apply streamlined analysis, how to identify judicial exceptions, and how to explain why additional claim elements do or do not provide 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity / Insignificant application
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that add only insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering or insignificant application steps) do not meaningfully limit a judicial exception and thus do not render the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and discussion: Cutting hair after first determining the hair style (In re Brown); printing or downloading generated menus (Ameranth). Some cases identify insignificant computer implementation as an example of insignificant extra-solution activity (Fort Props.; Bancorp Servs.). Examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why such limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim; e.g., storing data added to a process that only recites computing the area of a space does not add a meaningful limitation. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for more information about insignificant computer implementation and MPEP § 2106.07(a) for formulating rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of Use / Technological Environment limitation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely link the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (i.e., a 'field of use' limitation) generally do not amount to 'significantly more' and cannot integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic example: Parker v. Flook — limiting a formula to petrochemical/oil-refining fields did not make the claim eligible. Contrast: Diamond v. Diehr — specific limitations acting in concert (monitoring elapsed time, measuring temperature, repetitively calculating cure time, opening press automatically) provided eligibility. Recent examples where field-of-use limitations failed: Affinity Labs (limiting to cellular telephones), Mayo (limiting drug administration to a patient population), Bilski (participant-limited hedging process), FairWarning (computer execution environment), Intellectual Ventures (telephone network/Internet use), Electric Power Group (power-grid data), Genetic Techs. Ltd. (informing doctors to apply a law of nature), Capital One (communication medium like Internet/telephone), Ultramercial (Internet use for advertising-as-currency), buySAFE (computer/network or online-transaction limitation). Examiners should consider 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeable for eligibility analysis and note overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP § 2106.05(g)). For claim limitations that generally link the judicial exception to a particular technological environment, examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim (e.g., employing generic computer functions in a particular environment is insufficient). See MPEP § 2106.07(a) for examples of how to explain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) — when to use
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) where the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (for example, the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The streamlined analysis is for efficiency; its results must match the full Alice/Mayo analysis. If there is doubt whether applicant is seeking coverage for a judicial exception itself, the full analysis should be conducted. A claim eligible under Step 2A (Pathway B) or Step 2B (Pathway C) would also be eligible under the streamlined analysis. The record may show eligibility simply by absence of an eligibility rejection or include clarifying remarks. See MPEP § 2106 (subsection III) and MPEP § 2106.06 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility is self-evident — what qualifies
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is 'self-evidently' eligible when, viewed as a whole, it clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception such that others cannot practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: complex manufactured industrial products or processes that recite meaningful limitations alongside a judicial exception (e.g., a robotic arm assembly with a control system using certain mathematical relationships); nature-based products that do not attempt to tie up the nature-based product (e.g., artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral; cellphone with gold electrical contact; plastic chair with wood trim). If claims are a 'close call' as to whether they improve technology or computer functionality, perform the full eligibility analysis (BASCOM example). Only when clear improvement or self-evident eligibility exists should Pathway A be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear improvement to technology or computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are directed to clear improvements in technology or computer functionality may be not abstract and thus avoid the full eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit precedents: Enfish (self-referential table for a computer database) and McRO (automatic lip synchronization and facial expression animation) were found eligible because they claimed improvements to computer-related technology. Claims that clearly improve technology may be eligible at Pathway A or at Step 2A (Pathway B). If improvement is unclear or 'close call' (e.g., BASCOM's filtering content concept), the full Step 2B analysis should be used to determine whether claims amount to significantly more than an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections must be based on substantive law and review the whole record
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rejections must be grounded in the substantive law under 35 U.S.C. 101 as interpreted by judicial precedent, and examiners should review the entire record (specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law, prior art) before concluding eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination guidance, training, and examples discuss substantive law but do not themselves serve as a basis for rejection. Applicants may cite training materials or examples in arguments but should not be required to model claims after training examples. The substantive law on eligibility is discussed in MPEP §§ 2106.03–2106.06. The evaluation of eligibility should be claim-by-claim because dependent claims may add limitations that change the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim in an application must be considered separately for subject matter eligibility because claims do not automatically rise or fall with similar claims in an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an independent claim is determined ineligible, dependent claims may be eligible if they add limitations that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more; conversely, dependent claims may be ineligible even if the independent claim was deemed eligible. Examiners should evaluate each claim on its own merits and in view of the entire record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating a prima facie case for ineligibility and examiner burden
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is more likely than not that a claim does not satisfy eligibility criteria (Step 1 NO and/or Step 2B NO), the examiner should formulate an appropriate rejection that sets forth a prima facie case of ineligibility under the substantive law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prima facie concept allocates burdens: the initial burden is on the examiner to clearly and specifically explain why a claim is ineligible so the applicant has sufficient notice and can respond effectively. If applicant rebuts properly, the rejection should be withdrawn or the examiner must rebut in the next Office action. See MPEP § 2106.07(b) for response considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a Step 2A Prong One rejection (identify the judicial exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Step 2A Prong One rejection must identify the judicial exception by referring to what is recited in the claim and explain why it is considered an exception (e.g., identify the abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon and provide a reasoned rationale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim 'describes' but does not expressly set forth the exception, the rejection must explain what subject matter those limitations describe and why the described subject matter is a judicial exception. For abstract ideas, identify how the claim recites the abstract idea (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) as enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a Step 2A Prong Two rejection (integration into a practical application)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Step 2A Prong Two, the rejection should identify additional elements beyond the judicial exception and evaluate whether those elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rejection must specifically point to claim features/limitations/steps beyond the identified judicial exception and explain that either (1) there are no additional elements, or (2) the claim as a whole (considering additional elements individually and in combination) does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application using the considerations set forth in MPEP §§ 2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Examiners should give weight to all claimed additional elements in Prong Two, even if they represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a Step 2B rejection (inventive concept / 'significantly more')
rubrics_metrics.description: For Step 2B, the rejection must explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the examiner concludes certain claim elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing with one of the four options specified in Subsection III (e.g., factual findings, citation to evidence). The rejection should address both individual elements and their combination and explain why they fail to supply an 'inventive concept' that makes the claim eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish invention and apply broadest reasonable interpretation when formulating rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Before rejecting, examiners should determine what the applicant invented and establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claimed invention (see MPEP § 2111), then evaluate eligibility of each claim as a whole using MPEP § 2106 analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection, the Office action must provide an explanation as to why each claim is unpatentable that is sufficiently clear and specific to provide applicant sufficient notice and enable effective response. Subject matter eligibility rejections under Step 1 and Step 2 should follow the specific explanatory guidance for each step (see MPEP §§ 2106.03 and 2106.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution — state all non-cumulative reasons and bases in first Office action
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection is made, examiners should perform a complete examination for every claim under other patentability requirements and state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete examination should include consideration under 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, and issues of utility, inventorship, and double patenting (including non-statutory double patenting). This supports compact prosecution and avoids piecemeal rejections.
